title: Week 3 Mastery Quiz — Early Humanity and the Agricultural Revolution

questions.prompt: Which description best fits most Paleolithic communities?
choices: Large states organized around permanent capitals
Mobile or semi-mobile groups relying on hunting, gathering, fishing, and detailed environmental knowledge
Industrial cities supplied by mechanized agriculture
Settled farming villages dependent on written tax records
questions.explanation: For most of human history, Paleolithic communities were mobile or semi-mobile and relied on hunting, gathering, fishing, and deep environmental knowledge rather than settled agriculture.

questions.prompt: What does domestication mean in the context of the Neolithic transition?
choices: A sudden invention of agriculture in one location
The replacement of all wild foods by crops
The long-term process of selecting and managing plants or animals for human use
The creation of writing for farm records
questions.explanation: Domestication was a long-term process in which people increasingly selected, managed, and reproduced plants and animals for human purposes.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would most directly help an archaeologist infer that an early village stored agricultural surplus?
choices: Large storage pits containing concentrated plant remains
A modern textbook describing agriculture
A political border drawn on a present-day map
A later legend with no material connection to the site
questions.explanation: Storage pits and concentrated plant remains are material evidence that can support an inference about food storage and surplus, especially when interpreted in archaeological context.

questions.prompt: Why should historians avoid describing the Agricultural Revolution as one event that happened everywhere at the same time?
choices: Agriculture never changed human communities
All farming began in a single river valley
Written records prove every region adopted the same crops
Domestication developed gradually and independently in several regions, with many communities combining farming, hunting, and gathering for long periods
questions.explanation: The transition was uneven and gradual. Multiple regions developed agriculture independently, and mixed subsistence strategies continued for centuries.

questions.prompt: Which outcome best explains how agricultural surplus could encourage specialization?
choices: Stored food could support some people who spent more time on crafts, administration, trade, or other non-food-producing work
Surplus eliminated all differences in wealth
Specialization required communities to become mobile
Surplus prevented organized leadership from emerging
questions.explanation: When communities could store food beyond immediate needs, some members could spend more time on specialized work rather than producing food full time.

questions.prompt: A cemetery from an early farming village shows major differences in grave goods between burials. What is the most responsible inference?
choices: Every person had equal status
The community definitely had a monarchy
The differences may indicate social inequality or status distinctions, but additional evidence is needed to explain their exact meaning
Grave goods prove which crops the community grew
questions.explanation: Unequal grave goods can support an inference about status differences, but they do not by themselves prove a specific political system or explain the exact basis of inequality.

questions.prompt: Which comparison best reflects the evidence about possible costs and benefits of settled agriculture?
choices: Agriculture increased mobility while eliminating disease exposure
Agriculture could increase food storage and population while also increasing labor demands, disease exposure, land conflict, and inequality
Agriculture always improved nutrition for every person
Agriculture immediately ended hunting and gathering everywhere
questions.explanation: The agricultural transition created both opportunities and costs. Larger settlements and food storage coexisted with new labor burdens, disease risks, land claims, conflict, and unequal access to resources.

questions.prompt: Why is archaeology especially important for studying early human communities?
choices: Archaeology replaces the need for evidence
Archaeologists can directly observe the past
Archaeology proves all societies followed the same path
Material remains can provide evidence where written records are absent, limited, or represent only a narrow part of society
questions.explanation: For periods without extensive written records, material evidence such as tools, seeds, bones, structures, pollen, and human remains is essential for reconstructing past lifeways.

questions.prompt: A map shows several early centers of domestication in different world regions. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Agriculture developed independently in more than one region
All agriculture originated from a single universal center
Climate had no relationship to domestication
Every region domesticated the same species
questions.explanation: Evidence from multiple early centers supports the conclusion that agriculture and domestication developed independently in several regions rather than from one universal origin.

questions.prompt: Which thesis best answers the Week 3 essential question using historical complexity?
choices: Agriculture was entirely good because populations grew
Agriculture was entirely harmful because inequality existed

Agriculture increased food security and settlement in many places, but it also introduced new labor demands, disease risks, land conflicts, and inequalities, so its effects depended on community and context
Agriculture had no significant effect on human societies
questions.explanation: A strong historical thesis acknowledges multiple effects, avoids universal claims, and connects benefits and costs to evidence and context.

shortResponse.prompt: Using at least two specific pieces of Week 3 evidence, answer: Did agriculture improve human life, or did it exchange some freedoms for new forms of security and inequality? Your response must identify one benefit, one cost, and one limitation or uncertainty in the evidence.
shortResponse.exemplar: Full-credit work makes a defensible claim, accurately uses at least two Week 3 details such as storage, domestication, settlement, specialization, disease, labor, mobility, or inequality, explains both a benefit and a cost, and acknowledges one uncertainty or limit in the surviving evidence.
